messages.subject: Zero-inflated Poisson with over dispersion
parts:
Dear list,

I have this simple zero-inflated Poisson model with over dispersion, the model is as follows,

———————— model ————————
if y[i] = 0,        p(y[i] | mu[i]) = theta + (1-theta)Pois(0| exp(mu[i]) )
otherwise,      p(y[i] | mu[i]) = (1-theta)Pois(y[i]| exp(mu[i]) )

where

theta = inv_logit(-mu[i])

and

mu ~ normal(mu0,sigma)
———————— end of model ————————

My inference interest is only on the log-mean mu0 and the over-dispersion parameter sigma and I don’t care at all about the values of the mu[i]’s. However, I cannot figure out a way to marginalize them out so I leave them in the model. Below is how I wrote the model in stan

———————— stan model ————————
data {
     int<lower=0> N;
     int<lower=0> y[N];
}
parameters {
   real<lower=0> sigma;
   real mu0;
   real mu[N];
}
model {
      mu ~ normal(mu0,sigma);
      for (j in 1:N){
             if (y[j] == 0)
        increment_log_prob( log_sum_exp( bernoulli_log( 1,inv_logit(-mu[j] ) ),
bernoulli_log(0,inv_logit(-kappa*mu[j] ))
+ poisson_log( y[j],exp(mu[j]) ) ) );
             else
increment_log_prob( bernoulli_log(0,inv_logit(-mu[j] ))
+ poisson_log( y[j],exp(mu[j]) ) );
  }
}
———————— end of stan model ————————

However, when N = 1000 the running time starts to become really long. I guess part of the reason is because stan tries to save all the mu[i]’s whose total number equals the sample size. 

So my question is: is there a way to hack stan and let stan not save these mu[i]’s? Any other comments are also welcome.

Thanks for your time.

Best,
Eric Wang

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero-inflated Poisson with over dispersion
parts:
The typical solution for overdispersion in count data is
to use a negative binomial, which is a gamma-poisson
compound rather than the lognormal-Poisson you're going with.
I don't know if the lognormal form is important, but the gamma
version is available in marginalized form in a couple
negative-binomial implementations.

Also, I don't know why you'd use that mu in both the binomial
and in the Bernoulli and Poisson components.

If you do Poisson explicitly, I'd suggest

poisson_log_log(y, alpha) = poisson_log(y, exp(alpha))

- Bob

messages.author: 82a5c9fe6cf0d2bb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero-inflated Poisson with over dispersion
parts:
Hi Bob,

Thanks so much for the reply.

The typical solution for overdispersion in count data is
to use a negative binomial, which is a gamma-poisson
compound rather than the lognormal-Poisson you're going with.
I don't know if the lognormal form is important, but the gamma
version is available in marginalized form in a couple
negative-binomial implementations.

If I were to have just univariate count data then yes I can definitely use Negative-binomial distribution. But eventually I want to model multivariate count data and the log-normal form enables me to model the underlying variance-covariance structure which is my main inference focus. Is Negative-binomial (any other count distribution) capable of modeling the correlation structure of multivariate data?

Also, I don't know why you'd use that mu in both the binomial
and in the Bernoulli and Poisson components.
This comes from our prior belief of the data. Is having mu in both Bernoulli and Poisson harmful to MCMC?

If you do Poisson explicitly, I'd suggest

poisson_log_log(y, alpha)  = poisson_log(y, exp(alpha))

But eventually I want to model multivariate count data and the log-normal form enables me to model the underlying variance-covariance structure which is my main inference focus. Is Negative-binomial (any other count distribution) capable of modeling the correlation structure of multivariate data?

Not directly, as it's only univariate. You'd have to
introduce latent structure in the underlying linear predictor
(and/or overdispersion parameter) of the GLM.

> Also, I don't know why you'd use that mu in both the binomial
> and in the Bernoulli and Poisson components.
>
>
> This comes from our prior belief of the data. Is having mu in both Bernoulli and Poisson harmful to MCMC?

As long as the posterior is proper, it won't break HMC. I'm used
to seeing scale parameters in both means and variances for negative
binomial, but not for Bernoulli. But I don't have a huge amount of
experience in any of this.

- Bob
